section_summary: This section follows negotiations over Japan’s Petroleum Industry Law, especially its requirement that oil companies hold six months of stocks. American and British companies weigh a fixed storage ceiling, compensation, guarantees of future business, and Japanese financing while U.S. officials consider how to support the talks. A despatch also reports plans for coal liquefaction at Fushun.

people.name: Stanley K. Hornbeck
people.role: Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs

people.name: Walter Teagle
people.role: President, Standard Oil Company of New Jersey

people.name: Kurusu
people.role: Chief of the Bureau of Commercial Affairs, Japanese Foreign Office

people.name: Yoshino
people.role: Vice Minister for Commerce and Industry

people.name: Meyer
people.role: Local representative of Standard-Vacuum Oil Company

people.name: Ely
people.role: Local representative of Rising Sun Petroleum Company

subfiles.title: Meyer’s message on discussions with Kurusu and Yoshino
subfiles.about: Reports Japan’s refusal to change the storage law and its willingness to discuss compensation.
subfiles.summary: Kurusu says the law must stand, but Japan will consider proposals on compensation and safeguards against wider adoption of stock requirements.

subfiles.title: Instruction enclosing Tokyo despatch on the oil situation
subfiles.to: American Chargé d’Affaires ad interim, London
subfiles.about: Forwards a Tokyo despatch and enclosures concerning oil in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Sends the London mission a Tokyo despatch and its enclosures.

subfiles.title: Division note on Tokyo telegram No. 34
subfiles.about: Assesses Japan’s proposed fixed ceiling on required oil stocks.
subfiles.summary: The proposed fixed quantity may help foreign companies, though its lasting value is uncertain.

subfiles.title: Tokyo telegram No. 34 on oil storage negotiations
subfiles.about: Relays proposed terms for foreign companies to hold six months of oil stocks.
subfiles.summary: The Vice Minister says the law cannot change, but suggests a fixed maximum, compensation, and guarantees of future business. He warns that refusal could reduce foreign quotas and permit more Japanese refining capacity.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Walter Teagle on the Japanese Petroleum Law
subfiles.about: Records a telephone discussion of Japan’s storage proposal and coordination with British interests.
subfiles.summary: Teagle discusses a fixed storage amount and plans to consult London; Hornbeck urges the oil interests to remain united.

subfiles.title: Instruction enclosing oil-company conversation memoranda
subfiles.to: American Chargé d’Affaires ad interim, London
subfiles.about: Forwards three memoranda of conversations with American oil representatives.
subfiles.summary: Encloses memoranda dated February 10, 17, and 25.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Tokyo enclosing oil-company conversation memoranda
subfiles.about: Forwards three memoranda of conversations with American oil representatives.
subfiles.summary: Encloses memoranda dated February 10, 17, and 25.

subfiles.title: Tokyo telegram No. 42 forwarding Meyer’s reply
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo; message signed Meyer
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, for Reklawso, New York
subfiles.about: Explains objections to a London proposal for government ownership of emergency oil stocks.
subfiles.summary: Meyer considers the proposal legally feasible but politically impractical: it could humiliate Japan and jeopardize trading guarantees. He favors a compromise that permits government financing with less loss of face.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck letter forwarding Tokyo telegram No. 42
subfiles.about: Sends the Embassy telegram containing Meyer’s message for New York.
subfiles.summary: Forwards Tokyo’s February 27 telegram to Dundas.

subfiles.title: Copy of Tokyo telegram No. 42
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo; message signed Meyer
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, for Reklawso, New York
subfiles.about: Repeats Meyer’s objections to a London government-financing proposal.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate of the telegram on pages 11–12.

subfiles.title: Further copy of Tokyo telegram No. 42
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo; message signed Meyer
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, for Reklawso, New York
subfiles.about: Repeats Meyer’s objections to a London government-financing proposal.
subfiles.summary: Another copy of the telegram on pages 11–12.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck memorandum on talks with Parker and Goold
subfiles.about: Considers whether American companies should resist or negotiate compliance with Japan’s oil-storage law.
subfiles.summary: Parker and Goold describe differing British and American approaches and ask whether either could prejudice U.S. interests. Hornbeck favors continued American-British unity and considers the British course preferable. He cautions that an agreement with Japan might not secure the companies’ position in the long run.

subfiles.title: Brief for Hornbeck on Japanese control law developments
subfiles.about: Introduces attached cables and memoranda on changing company positions.
subfiles.summary: Notes British interest in obtaining a definite Japanese proposal before offering concessions.

subfiles.title: Standard-Vacuum memorandum seeking State Department advice
subfiles.about: Asks about the consequences of resisting or conditionally accepting six-month storage.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum outlines British terms for three-month stocks and possible Japanese compensation for additional storage. It asks whether deliberate non-compliance or a negotiated six-month arrangement would prejudice U.S. interests.

subfiles.title: Outgoing cablegram form
subfiles.about: Contains an outgoing cablegram form with no legible message.
subfiles.summary: No substantive message is legible.

subfiles.title: Outgoing cablegram form
subfiles.about: Contains a second outgoing cablegram form with no legible message.
subfiles.summary: No substantive message is legible.

subfiles.title: Yokohama cable on Kurusu’s reply
subfiles.about: Reports Kurusu’s response on storage requirements and compensation.
subfiles.summary: The damaged copy appears to duplicate the January 21 message on page 1.

subfiles.title: New York cable to Yokohama
subfiles.about: Addresses the companies’ objections to financing emergency stocks.
subfiles.summary: The copy is heavily damaged. Its substance is reflected in the clearer February 5 enclosure on page 64.

subfiles.title: Japan memorandum on possible failure of negotiations
subfiles.about: Sets out possible responses if Japan will not modify the Petroleum Law.
subfiles.summary: British interests reject financing six months of emergency stocks. They consider Japanese financing, continued trade without compliance, and eventual withdrawal, while preferring to pursue the five-point memorandum.

subfiles.title: Instruction to London enclosing control-law papers
subfiles.to: American Chargé d’Affaires ad interim, London
subfiles.about: Forwards papers concerning the Japanese oil situation.
subfiles.summary: Sends London copies of papers cited in a conversation memorandum.

subfiles.title: Japan Petroleum Control Law understanding
subfiles.about: Records a proposed understanding on quotas, stocks, prices, and discrimination.
subfiles.summary: Outlines the five-point understanding discussed with Japanese officials in April 1935.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Tokyo enclosing control-law papers
subfiles.about: Forwards briefs, cables, and memoranda on the oil situation.
subfiles.summary: Lists six enclosures concerning oil-company negotiations.

subfiles.title: Note to the Secretary on petroleum-law papers
subfiles.about: Calls attention to selected pages of attached petroleum-law papers.
subfiles.summary: Recommends that the Secretary read the first and last two pages.

subfiles.title: Telephone conversation with Parker
subfiles.about: Records Hornbeck’s informal answer to Standard-Vacuum’s questions.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck conveys his preference for the British approach and stresses a united front. He says the companies should decide their course and doubts the Department would put its advice in writing.

subfiles.title: Dundas letter enclosing London and Yokohama cables
subfiles.about: Sends recent company cables about Japanese storage negotiations.
subfiles.summary: Explains that London and Yokohama messages crossed and that a reply is pending.

subfiles.title: London cable proposing Japanese-owned storage
subfiles.about: Explores government financing and ownership of additional tanks and stocks.
subfiles.summary: London proposes that Japan own non-commercial storage while companies manage it and may later buy useful tanks and stocks. It asks local representatives for views but instructs them not to present the idea to Japan yet.

subfiles.title: Yokohama cable reporting Yoshino’s position
subfiles.about: Reports proposed conditions for accepting fixed quantities of six-month stocks.
subfiles.summary: Yoshino says the law must remain, but suggests a fixed maximum, compensation, and business guarantees. Yokohama urges a prompt proposal with government financing before quotas and refinery applications are decided.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck acknowledgment to Dundas
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the cables enclosed with Dundas’s February 25 letter.
subfiles.summary: Says the Yokohama cable agrees substantially with the Embassy’s report.

subfiles.title: Document file note on oil negotiations
subfiles.about: Cross-references a Grew report on negotiations over storage requirements.
subfiles.summary: Points to a January 18 Grew report filed elsewhere.

subfiles.title: Extract on American oil interests in Japan
subfiles.about: Recaps December 1935 exchanges over the five-point memorandum and stockholding.
subfiles.summary: Japanese officials reject changing storage requirements and say the earlier memorandum was not binding. Kurusu seeks possible quota and price guarantees that might support a settlement.

subfiles.title: Tokyo telegram No. 64 on proposed storage company
subfiles.about: Asks whether the Embassy should join talks on an oil-company financing proposal.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy says direct participation would imply official approval and will abstain unless instructed.

subfiles.title: Department telegram No. 30 to Tokyo
subfiles.about: Authorizes informal diplomatic support for oil-company talks.
subfiles.summary: Suggests that American and British diplomats informally convey interest in negotiations without joining the conference.

subfiles.title: Division note on Tokyo despatch No. 1692
subfiles.about: Highlights a planned coal-liquefaction plant at Fushun.
subfiles.summary: Notes Japanese plans for a Navy-supported South Manchuria Railway plant producing oil from coal, despite doubtful commercial profitability.

subfiles.title: Tokyo despatch No. 1692 on American oil interests
subfiles.about: Reports storage negotiations and Japanese coal-liquefaction plans.
subfiles.summary: Kurusu considers a fixed ceiling on oil stocks, compensation, and trading guarantees, but no settlement has emerged. The despatch describes rejected financing ideas and explains the companies’ concern about international precedent. It also reports plans for a subsidized coal-to-oil plant at Fushun.

subfiles.title: February 5 oil-company message to local representatives
subfiles.from: London and New York oil-company headquarters
subfiles.about: Explains why financing emergency stocks conflicts with the companies’ trading position.
subfiles.summary: Asks representatives to seek a solution through the five-point memorandum or another means.

subfiles.title: Notes of Foreign Office meeting
subfiles.about: Records Kurusu’s discussion with Ely and Meyer about a fixed stockholding ceiling.
subfiles.summary: Kurusu argues that a fixed number of gallons, compensation, and guarantees could reconcile the law with company concerns. Ely and Meyer respond that financing non-commercial stocks would still set a dangerous precedent. Kurusu says he will consult Yoshino but rejects government financing.

subfiles.title: Instruction to London enclosing despatch No. 1692
subfiles.to: American Chargé d’Affaires ad interim, London
subfiles.about: Forwards Grew’s February 20 despatch and its enclosures.
subfiles.summary: Sends London the Tokyo report on oil negotiations.

subfiles.title: Dundas letter quoting March 7 company cable
subfiles.about: Describes a proposal for an independently financed Japanese storage company.
subfiles.summary: Dundas quotes a joint London and New York cable proposing a local company to finance excess stocks, with gradual retirement of its financing as stocks become commercially useful. He requests the Embassy’s moral support for discussions with Kurusu and Yoshino.

subfiles.title: Yokohama cable on timing of a concrete proposal
subfiles.about: Urges a proposal before Japan decides the next quarter’s quotas.
subfiles.summary: The damaged cable warns that delay could weaken the companies’ bargaining position. It discusses government financing and reports renewed interest in merging Japanese oil-company sales organizations.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck letter to Dundas on Embassy support
subfiles.about: Explains the Department’s response to the proposed Japanese financing arrangement.
subfiles.summary: Says the proposal merits Japanese consideration and describes instructions for informal American and British diplomatic representations.

subfiles.title: Dundas acknowledgment of Hornbeck’s support
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Hornbeck’s letter about instructions to Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Thanks Hornbeck for the Department’s assistance.

subfiles.title: Division note on Tokyo telegram No. 73
subfiles.about: Notes a March 20 deadline for an oil agreement.
subfiles.summary: Records the new March 20 deadline; no action required.

subfiles.title: Tokyo telegram No. 73 on negotiations and quota deadline
subfiles.about: Reports diplomatic representations and Japan’s response to the storage-company plan.
subfiles.summary: American and British diplomats make informal representations after company representatives present their plan. Kurusu doubts an independent storage company is feasible because compensation is inadequate and says a decision is needed before March 20 quotas are set.
